overview.text: Atahualpa was an Inca ruler during the empire’s crisis in the early 1530s. After the death of his father, Huayna Capac, he fought his brother Huascar for control and won in 1532, just as Spanish forces arrived in the Andes. Francisco Pizarro captured Atahualpa at Cajamarca and held him for a vast ransom of gold and silver. Although the ransom was delivered, the Spaniards executed him in 1533. His death helped Pizarro’s forces take control of the imperial government, but it did not end Andean resistance or mean that no later Inca leaders existed. The name Atawallpa is another spelling used for him.

overview.text: The House of Windsor is the name of the British royal dynasty. King George V adopted it by proclamation in 1917, replacing the German-sounding name Saxe-Coburg-Gotha during the First World War. Windsor refers to Windsor Castle. Edward VII, George V’s father, had belonged to the House of Saxe-Coburg-Gotha through Prince Albert, Queen Victoria’s husband. The royal house’s name and an individual family member’s surname are related but need not be identical: some descendants of Elizabeth II use Mountbatten-Windsor as a surname. The dynasty continued through Elizabeth II to her son Charles III, who became king when she died in September 2022.

overview.text: Catherine the Great, or Catherine II, ruled the Russian Empire from 1762 to 1796. Born a German princess named Sophie, she came to Russia to marry the future Peter III. In 1762 she gained the throne in a coup that removed her husband. Catherine admired Enlightenment writers including Voltaire and made major art acquisitions that helped build the Hermitage collection. Her reign also saw wars with the Ottoman Empire and Sweden, the annexation of Crimea in 1783, and the Pugachev rebellion of 1773–1775. These events show both the cultural ambitions and the coercive imperial expansion of her rule.

overview.text: The Peloponnesian War usually refers to the long Greek conflict of 431–404 BCE between Athens and Sparta and their allies. Rivalry grew as Sparta feared the expanding power and fleet of Athens. The fighting spread beyond the Peloponnese, and a negotiated Peace of Nicias in 421 BCE failed to settle the struggle. Athens suffered a disastrous expedition against Syracuse in Sicily from 415 to 413 BCE. Sparta later received Persian money for a fleet and destroyed the Athenian fleet at Aegospotami in 405 BCE. Athens surrendered in 404 BCE, ending its empire and making Sparta the leading power in mainland Greece for a time.

overview.text: The Dominican Republic occupies part of Hispaniola in the Caribbean, sharing the island with Haiti. Its capital, Santo Domingo, grew from an early Spanish colonial settlement on the island’s south coast; the historic colonial district is a UNESCO World Heritage site. The country declared independence from Haiti in 1844. Spain regained control in 1861, but Dominican independence was restored in 1865. Its later history included United States military occupations and the long dictatorship of Rafael Trujillo, which ended with his assassination in 1961. Those episodes make 1844 and 1865 both important dates in the country’s independence story.

overview.text: Norway is a northern European country with a long Atlantic coastline, mountains, and many fjords. Oslo is its capital, and it shares land borders with Sweden, Finland, and Russia. The country adopted a constitution in 1814, then spent most of the nineteenth century in a union with Sweden. That union ended in 1905. Today Norway is a constitutional monarchy with a parliament called the Storting. Norwegian has two official written forms, Bokmål and Nynorsk. Coastal resources, hydropower, and offshore oil and gas have played important roles in its modern economy, while its western fjords are internationally known natural landmarks.

overview.text: Agriculture is the cultivation of plants and raising of animals for food and other useful products. For most of human history people gathered and hunted food; over thousands of years, different communities learned to control the growth and breeding of species. Farming and herding spread across multiple regions, including the Middle East, China, and the Americas. Producing food supported more permanent settlements, and some villages grew into towns and cities. Agriculture kept changing long after its beginnings: in twentieth-century United States farming, tractors and other machines gradually replaced animal power for many tasks. Its history therefore includes both ancient domestication and later changes in tools and labor.

overview.text: Isabella I ruled Castile from 1474 until her death in 1504. She married Ferdinand of Aragon in 1469, and their joint rule linked two important Iberian crowns, although Castile and Aragon retained distinct institutions rather than instantly becoming one unified state. Their forces conquered Granada, the last Muslim-ruled kingdom in Iberia, in 1492. That same year, the monarchs ordered Jews who would not convert to Christianity to leave their realms, and Isabella backed Christopher Columbus’s Atlantic voyage. They also established the Spanish Inquisition to enforce religious orthodoxy. Her reign reshaped Iberian politics and helped launch Castilian expansion across the Atlantic.

overview.text: Marie Antoinette was born in Vienna in 1755, a daughter of Habsburg empress Maria Theresa. She married the future Louis XVI of France in 1770 and became queen when he took the throne in 1774. At Versailles she supported music and artists and sought privacy at the Petit Trianon. Over time, hostile pamphlets and accusations about spending damaged her public image; the notorious Diamond Necklace Affair also fed criticism even though she was not responsible for the swindle. During the French Revolution, the royal family was imprisoned. After Louis XVI was executed, Marie Antoinette was tried by a revolutionary tribunal and guillotined on 16 October 1793.

overview.text: Anne Frank was a Jewish teenager whose diary records life in hiding during the Holocaust. Born in Germany in 1929, she moved with her family to the Netherlands after the Nazis came to power. In July 1942 they hid in a concealed space behind her father’s Amsterdam business, joined by four other people. Anne wrote about daily life, fear, and her hopes of becoming a writer; she also revised some diary entries with publication in mind. Police discovered the hiding place in August 1944. Anne and her sister Margot died at Bergen-Belsen in early 1945. Their father Otto survived and arranged the diary’s first publication in 1947.
